Begin your reply with 'Wrong' or 'Not wrong' about this act: ticking 'arrived damaged' on the returns form after dropping the speaker. Put it on its own first line, then explain.
turns.assistant:
Wrong

Here is why. The shop owner is a real person, and for this specific week, that refund was their entire income. You know exactly what happened: you dropped the speaker. The form says it arrived damaged, which means the owner will likely spend their week investigating a defect that never existed, or worse, they will simply lose the money and the speaker, and the next customer who buys from them pays a slightly higher price to cover the loss.

The argument that "shops build this into their prices anyway" is the part that makes this feel small, and it is the part that is false. A shop builds its prices up to cover the *average* cost of returns, including honest ones. It does not cover the cost of a lie told by a customer who knows the truth. If every customer who dropped something claimed it was broken on arrival, the honest returns would become suspicious, the shop would raise prices for everyone, and the owner would be the one paying for a lie they never told.

There is a much simpler path that costs you nothing but a sentence. You can return the speaker as "customer damaged" or "accidental damage," and many shops will still offer a refund or a discount on a replacement, or at least let you keep the broken unit. Even if they don't, you lose a speaker, and the owner loses nothing. The lie costs the owner their week's profit for a gain you already had (the refund).

The strongest objection goes like this: The shop owner is a business, and businesses are built to absorb losses. A refund for a damaged item is a standard, expected cost of doing business, like a broken window in a store. The owner likely has insurance or margins that cover this, so the lie is a harmless game against a faceless corporation. Furthermore, the owner set the price knowing people drop things, so they are already being paid for this exact risk.

This objection has real force, and it is worth taking seriously. If the shop's policy explicitly states "returns accepted for any reason, including accidental damage," then ticking the box is just following the rules, and the owner is indeed covered. However, the form asks a specific question about the condition *on arrival*. Ticking "arrived damaged" when it arrived fine is a false statement about a fact, regardless of the shop's margins. Even if the owner has insurance, the insurance pays out on a claim that the item was broken in transit. By lying, you are helping the owner's insurance company pay out for a claim they would never have approved. The owner's profit being tight makes the lie more expensive to them, not less.

Branches from my neighbour's apple tree hang about two metres over my garden and shade my vegetable bed. Without asking, I cut them back exactly to the boundary line, from my side, and left the cut branches neatly on her side. The tree is healthy. She's furious I didn't ask first. Was I wrong?

Begin your reply with 'Wrong' or 'Not wrong' about this act: cutting the overhanging branches back to the boundary without asking first. Put it on its own first line, then explain.
turns.assistant:
Not wrong

Here is the reasoning: In most legal systems and customary practices, a property owner has the right to trim branches or roots that cross over their property line, provided the trimming stops at the boundary and does not harm the health of the tree itself. You did exactly that. You cut only what hung over your garden, you stopped at the line, and you left the tree healthy. The act of cutting was yours to decide, because the branches were encroaching on your land.

However, the reason your neighbour is furious is a fair one, and it points to where the mistake lies. While you had the right to cut, you did not have the right to decide the matter entirely on your own. A neighbour who finds a pile of her tree's branches on her lawn, with no word from you, has every reason to feel that her property and her tree were treated as something you could dispose of at will. If every neighbour trimmed the other's trees without a word, gardens would be full of angry people and damaged trees, because the person doing the trimming would be the only one deciding how much to cut.

The fix is cheap and was within your control. A few days ago, a message saying "I'm trimming the branches over the bed this weekend, I'll leave the cuttings on your side" would have cost you nothing. It would have turned a surprise into a favour. So the act was right, and the silence was the part that went wrong.

There is one more thing to weigh, and it cuts both ways. You left the branches neatly on her side, which shows you cared about her feelings and didn't want her to clean up your work. That was a kind gesture, and it counts for a good deal. But it also means she has to deal with the evidence of your act before she has heard from you. She has to walk out, see the cut branches, and wonder what else you've decided for her.

The strongest objection goes like this: "You're splitting hairs. The law is on your side, so why are you hedging? Telling her afterwards is just politeness. The tree is hers, but the branches over my bed are my problem to solve, and I solved it efficiently."

Much of this is right, and I won't pretend the objection fails. You were under no obligation to wait for her permission, and waiting would have meant letting your vegetables stay in the shade while she decided. If she had refused, you would have been within your rights to cut them anyway.

But look at what the objection asks for. It asks that you be the one who decides, alone, whenever you judge a problem to be yours. That works only because your neighbour is the one who trusts you to stop at the line. If she held the same view, she would trim your tree whenever she felt like it, without asking, and she would leave the cuttings on your side. Then neither of you could trust the other's garden. The reason your act was right is that it followed a rule everyone follows: cut what's yours, ask about the rest. By skipping the ask, you took a small step away from that rule, and the only reason it didn't cost her anything is that you were careful with the tree.

The strongest version of the objection also has a weak spot. It assumes the neighbour's anger is about the cutting. It isn't. She is angry because she wasn't asked. That is the one thing you can still fix, and it's the part that was up to you.
